# Corvo Labs hero image prompts (15 posts, ChatGPT Images)

Updated 2026-09-29: Jake has selected all 15 final hero images and the raven character sheet. Revised prompts for 1–6 and Jake's second iteration for 8 are retained verbatim. The selected masters are recorded below; image generation is complete.

## A. How to run this in ChatGPT

### Approved references

All reference files are in this directory:

- `raven-character-sheet.png` — approved mascot identity, anatomy, proportions, feather construction, and role flexibility.
- `article-01-hero.png` through `article-07-hero.png`, and `article-08-image.png` through `article-15-image.png` — the 15 selected hero masters. Keep these selections and filenames.
- For a character scene, use `article-04-hero.png` as the general paper and lighting reference. For a denser workshop or map scene, `article-03-hero.png` is also useful.
- Both detailed scenes and isolated objects are representative. Match materials and visual clarity; composition can vary with the story.
- Article 7's photographic hand is an accepted exception. Ordinary human elements should be made of paper.

### Generation recipe for future revisions

All 15 hero masters are now selected. Further generation is unnecessary for this publication package. For any future revision, attach the approved raven sheet as image 1 and a selected hero as image 2, binding character identity and paper construction separately. Use one scene per request and evaluate the visible action or reveal at thumbnail size.

Jake's **Revised Prompt iteration 2** for article 8 records the selected workshop scene. It makes the role, gaze, costume, instrumentation, and physical connections explicit. Modern sensors and computer monitors are allowed when fabricated in the same matte paper world, with subdued illustrative graphics and no real statistics or luminous screen effects.

### Export and publishing integration

The final deliverable for each post is **1600×900 WebP under 150 KB**, at:

`corvo-labs-enhanced/public/images/blog/<slug>/hero.webp`

Resize proportionally and crop as needed; inspect the selected image before choosing a crop. Tune WebP quality to meet the size limit without losing the paper texture. Do not stretch a nonmatching source ratio.

```yaml
coverImage: "/images/blog/<slug>/hero.webp"
coverImageAlt: "<description of the selected image>"
```

The existing site inspection found an uncropped, relatively small article hero and centered `object-cover` list thumbnails. Therefore keep the key interaction in the center band, while allowing the whole scene to fill the canvas. Recheck the rendered pages during publishing. Alt text below records the selected images and Jake's approved wording.

The prior site inspection also found a broken OG fallback image and a localhost `metadataBase`. These need to be raised with Jake before relying on social previews; they have not been fixed as part of this prompt revision.

## B. Shared art direction

Familiar metaphors are encouraged. A raven can represent the editor, evaluator, engineer, reader, or another participant the individual story needs. An overarching mascot narrative is optional. A scene may be dense when its details explain the story, or sparse when one object carries the reveal.

The base palette is cohesive, with purposeful color exceptions. Short useful labels are allowed. Documents and charts are illustrative. The approved images take precedence over restrictive wording inside their historical prompts.

### Current style block

This block is already expanded in prompts 8–15, so those prompts can be copied directly.

```
Create one wide 16:9 editorial illustration built from cut and layered matte paper. Use crisp hand-cut edges with occasional slight deckling, visible paper tooth and fibers, believable paper thickness, broad feather or object layers, and restrained contact shadows. Photograph the paper construction under soft, diffuse upper-left daylight with neutral white balance. Everything, including clothes, tools, plants, furniture, and any human elements, belongs to the same tactile paper world.

Use warm-neutral off-white #ECE9E2, charcoal #22272B, slate teal #2E5B60, and pale sage #B7C4B4 as the base palette. Burnt copper #C2612C provides purposeful emphasis; it can appear on more than one related detail. Small additional material colors are allowed when they make a familiar subject recognizable. Keep the background neutral off-white without a yellow cast.

Stage a recognizable physical scene with a clear action, relationship, or reveal. Give the main subject enough scale and specific detail to have substance. Supporting detail should explain the scene. Keep the decisive interaction near the vertical center so a wide thumbnail crop retains the story; secondary scenery can extend toward the edges. Use broad silhouettes and clear visual hierarchy, with no need to confine the entire scene to a tiny central cluster.

Where the raven appears, match the approved character sheet: charcoal layered feather shapes, substantial slate-teal beak, off-white eyes with dark pupils, compact body, tapered tail, slender bird legs and toes, and wings that can grip tools through feather-like fingers. Keep its face, proportions, and paper construction consistent. Clothing, equipment, posture, and expression may change for its role. It is competent, curious, and composed, with quiet whimsy.

Use only readable text explicitly requested for this scene. Documents, charts, and diagrams use illustrative blocks, lines, and shapes; they carry no real statistics, quotations, or evidence. No extra captions, logos, or watermarks. Avoid glowing brains, robots, circuit-board decoration, holograms, neon, stock medical or legal props, glossy materials, gradients, cinematic lighting, and a smooth 3D-render finish. One image only.
```

### 1. The digest was cited and still wrong

- **Slug / path:** `the-digest-was-cited-and-still-wrong` -> `.../public/images/blog/the-digest-was-cited-and-still-wrong/hero.webp`
- **Selected master:** `article-01-hero.png` — approved by Jake.
- **Current concept:** Raven archer and missed arrows.
- **Current alt text:** "Even with all the right equipment, sometimes you still miss the mark."

The original brief below is retained for history. The **Revised Prompt** records the final direction; older constraints and descriptions do not override the selected image.
- **Concept:** Everything was sourced and supported, and it still missed the mark.
- **Metaphor (from the article):** grounded and useful are two different tests. A neat, fully cited stack aimed just off the real target.
- **Original prompt (superseded):**

```
[PASTE STYLE BLOCK]

Use: blog hero illustration, 16:9 wide landscape, one image only.
Concept: Everything was sourced and supported, and it still missed the mark.
Scene: a tidy stack of slate-teal paper cards on the left, each connected by a fine teal thread to a single folded off-white page; at the right, a set of concentric cut-paper rings (sage, charcoal, off-white) forms a round target.
Subject placement: the card stack and folded page in the left half of the central area, the ring target in the right half of the central area, both inside the central 60 percent of the width; the thread runs in a straight line across and ends just beside the target, clearly missing the center by a small gap. The burnt-copper element is the first read; all other forms are quieter supporting weight.
Details: perfectly aligned cards and crisp thread; the burnt-copper accent is a small round center piece of the target, sitting untouched.
Constraints: No text, letters, numbers, labels, captions, logos, trademarks or watermark anywhere in the image, and no extra text. No people, no arrow graphics. Keep the center protected with clean margin around it; favor simplicity over detail. 16:9 wide, no text.
```

- **Variations:** "Fewer cards, four at most." / "Make the gap between the thread end and the target center more noticeable." / "Flatten the rings into three layers only."
- **Original alt text (superseded):** "A neat stack of paper cards threaded to a folded page, with the thread ending just beside the center of a ring target."

#### Revised Prompt
Create ONE wide 16:9 editorial blog hero illustration.

CORE IDEA
A superbly equipped raven archer has everything needed to succeed—specialized optics, an excellent bow, carefully prepared arrows—but has still missed the actual goal. The visual metaphor is “good tools and support do not guarantee the right outcome.”

Show this through one immediately readable scene, not a diagram: a confident, well-equipped raven on the left, facing a tilted archery target on the right. Three previously fired arrows have struck the target well away from its untouched bullseye.

The irony should come from the contrast between the archer’s impressive equipment and the conspicuously poor results. Do not make the raven look foolish, confused, or incompetent.

STYLE AND MATERIALS
Layered cut-paper still life, photographed as a clean editorial studio image. Every element—including the raven, its equipment, the arrows, and the target—is constructed from matte cut paper.

Use crisp hand-cut, very slightly deckled edges, visible paper thickness, fine fibers, paper tooth, and gentle grain. Build forms from a few broad overlapping paper shapes, generally two to four principal layers per component. Use subtle edge and contact shading to reveal the layers, not dramatic cast shadows or artificial drop shadows.

The result should feel tactile and handcrafted, not like a glossy 3D render, a realistic animal photograph, or a flat vector illustration.

Soft, diffuse, even daylight from the upper left. Neutral white balance; no yellow cast. Everything in sharp focus. Camera nearly straight-on, with only enough perspective to reveal the target’s angle and the paper construction.

PALETTE
Use only:
- Warm-neutral off-white #ECE9E2 for the background and target’s inner area.
- Charcoal #22272B for the raven, dark target ring, and small structural details.
- Deep slate teal #2E5B60 for the cloak, bow, and arrow shafts.
- Pale sage #B7C4B4 for the monocle housing, equipment accents, arrow fletching, and outer target ring.
- Burnt copper #C2612C on exactly ONE element: the small, untouched bullseye.

No other copper details anywhere.

COMPOSITION
Wide 16:9 landscape with a large cropped raven occupying the left side and a smaller, fully visible target on the right.

Crop the raven’s torso and cloak naturally at the left and bottom edges. Keep its head, monocle, working wings, and entire recurve bow visible. The raven should feel substantial and close to the viewer, not like a small icon floating in the middle of the canvas.

Leave a generous expanse of clean off-white negative space between the bow and the target. Keep the target comfortably inside the right edge, with breathing room above and below it.

Visual sequence: equipped raven → bow and direction of shooting → missed shots → untouched copper bullseye.

RAVEN ARCHER
An anthropomorphic raven or crow in profile, facing right. Use a simplified, graphic paper-cut silhouette: a strong charcoal beak, angular head shape, a few broad feather-shaped layers, and wing-like arms. No realistic individual feathers or human hands.

Equip it with three clearly readable features:
1. An oversized specialist monocle scope over its visible eye, made from concentric pale-sage paper rings around a dark teal lens, with a simple strap around the head.
2. An elegant, dramatically curved recurve bow in deep slate teal, with a few restrained pale-sage grip details.
3. A small shoulder quiver containing spare arrows with pale-sage fletching.

Add a simple deep-teal ranger-like cloak and minimal straps to complete the well-equipped silhouette. These should support the character rather than become decorative clutter.

The raven holds the bow with one wing-like arm and draws the string with the other. One arrow is nocked, aimed toward the right. Make the bow, string, grip, and arrow physically coherent and easy to read.

The character should feel capable, composed, and slightly whimsical—not aggressive, slapstick, or cartoonishly expressive.

TARGET AND MISSED SHOTS
On the right, show a freestanding circular archery target turned partly toward the raven. Its face is visibly angled in perspective, so its circular rings read as nested vertical ellipses. Show a little paper thickness and a simple charcoal support behind it.

Construct the target from three broad concentric paper areas:
- Pale-sage outer ring.
- Charcoal middle ring.
- Off-white inner area.
Plus a small burnt-copper center piece.

Show exactly THREE previously fired arrows embedded in the target’s outer areas, clearly far from the bullseye. Arrange them around the upper and lower outer regions so the misses are obvious at thumbnail size.

All three arrows must visibly originate from the raven’s side: their points enter the target from the left, with their shafts and feathered tails extending back toward the left. No arrow should appear to have been fired from the right.

“Missing the goal” means striking the outer target rather than the center—not merely stopping just short of the bullseye. Leave the entire off-white inner area and copper center visibly untouched and unobstructed.

These three embedded arrows are separate from the single arrow currently nocked in the bow and the spare arrows in the quiver.

TONE AND SIMPLICITY
Precise, quiet, trustworthy editorial illustration with a slightly whimsical character. One clear visual story. Broad silhouettes and restrained detail that remain readable at thumbnail size.

Do not add explanatory symbols, source cards, connecting threads, motion trails, scenery, or extra props.

EXCLUSIONS
No text, letters, numbers, writing-like marks, labels, captions, logos, trademarks, or watermarks.
No humans or human hands.
No diagram arrows; only the physical archery arrows described above.
No robots, circuit boards, screens, holograms, glowing lenses, neon, gradients, lens flare, shiny metal, plastic surfaces, or decorative clutter.

### 2. Search APIs are not an editorial strategy

- **Slug / path:** `search-apis-are-not-an-editorial-strategy` -> `.../public/images/blog/search-apis-are-not-an-editorial-strategy/hero.webp`
- **Selected master:** `article-02-hero.png` — approved by Jake.
- **Current concept:** A descending news-sorting system.
- **Current alt text:** "Paper news cards pass through a descending series of labeled sieves and conveyors into a collection bucket."

The original brief below is retained for history. The **Revised Prompt** records the final direction; older constraints and descriptions do not override the selected image.
- **Concept:** Three search providers, one week of news, three very different catches.
- **Metaphor (from the article):** Brave, Firecrawl and LangSearch run against the same window, sorted into strict, provisional and undated tiers.
- **Original prompt (superseded):**

```
[PASTE STYLE BLOCK]

Use: blog hero illustration, 16:9 wide landscape, one image only.
Concept: Three search providers, one week of news, three very different catches.
Scene: three round cut-paper sieves side by side, seen from the front and slightly above, all held over one shared heap of thin pale paper slips.
Subject placement: the three sieves in a row across the center, about 60 percent of the image width; the heap of slips low and centered beneath them. The burnt-copper element is the first read; all other forms are quieter supporting weight.
Details: the left sieve has a fine, dense pattern of small holes; the middle sieve has larger, sparser holes; the right sieve has almost no holes. Below each sieve is a small pile of slips of different sizes and tones: the left pile tidy, the middle mixed, the right a few stray slips. One tiny slip in burnt copper sits in the left pile.
Constraints: No text, letters, numbers, labels, captions, logos, trademarks or watermark anywhere in the image, and no extra text. No people, no liquid, no machines. Keep the center protected with clean margin around it; favor simplicity over detail. 16:9 wide, no text.
```

- **Variations:** "Make the hole patterns more clearly different between the three sieves." / "Reduce the shared heap to a single low band of slips." / "Use flat circles with cut holes and no rims for a cleaner look."
- **Original alt text (superseded):** "Three paper sieves with different hole patterns catching different piles of paper slips."


#### Revised Prompt
Create one blog hero illustration in a wide 16:9 landscape format.

CONCEPT
A mixed stream of news is sifted into three editorial categories: Big Stories, Medium Reads, and News Nuggets. Show this as a whimsical but clearly understandable paper-cut sorting system descending diagonally from the upper left to the lower right.

The story should read immediately: all the news enters together; large stories stay in the first sieve-container; medium stories stay in the second; the smallest news nuggets reach the final collection bucket. The paper pieces are being sorted by size, not shredded or transformed.

STYLE
Layered cut-paper still life, photographed as a clean editorial studio image. Everything is constructed from matte, tactile paper: the buckets, sieve-containers, conveyor belts, rollers, and news cards.

Use crisp hand-cut, very slightly deckled edges, visible paper thickness, fine fibers, subtle paper tooth, and gentle grain. Build forms from two to four thin paper layers, with shallow folded-paper rims and sidewalls where needed. Show restrained, soft contact shading that reveals the layers without heavy drop shadows. The result should feel like a handmade paper assemblage, not a glossy 3D render, vector infographic, or realistic industrial machine.

View the scene from the front and slightly above, so the open containers, sieve holes, and cards are clearly visible. Keep everything in sharp focus, without lens distortion.

Use soft, diffuse, even daylight from the upper left, with neutral white balance and no yellow cast.

PALETTE
Limit the palette to:
- Warm-neutral off-white background: #ECE9E2
- Charcoal: #22272B
- Deep slate teal: #2E5B60
- Pale sage: #B7C4B4
- Burnt copper: #C2612C

Use burnt copper only for the “All the News” input bucket. This bucket is the main color accent and the first visual read. No copper cards or additional copper accents.

COMPOSITION
Arrange the entire system as a clear descending staircase across the landscape canvas, starting in the upper left and ending in the lower right.

Use most of the available width while keeping every object fully inside the frame with comfortable outer margins. Preserve generous open background above and to the right of the middle stages, and below and to the left. Let the diagonal flow create the composition; do not squeeze everything into a small central cluster.

There are exactly four containers: one input bucket, two combined sieve-containers, and one final solid collection bucket. There are exactly two conveyor belts.

UPPER LEFT — “All the News”
A burnt-copper paper bucket is tilted downward and to the right, pouring a lively but controlled stream of mixed-size paper cards into the first sieve-container.

The cards are blank, mostly rectangular or square, with subtly irregular hand-cut edges. Include three visibly distinct sizes: large cards, medium cards, and tiny pieces. Use off-white, pale sage, and deep slate teal for the cards.

Print “All the News” clearly on the bucket’s visible side.

FIRST STAGE — “Big Stories”
Below and to the right of the input bucket is a broad, shallow, deep-slate-teal sieve-container. Its elliptical opening reveals a perforated base with large, clearly visible circular holes.

The sieve and collection container are one integrated object, not separate objects stacked together. Its front paper sidewall is labeled “Big Stories.”

Several large cards remain visibly inside, too large to pass through the holes. Medium and small cards fall out through its bottom onto the first conveyor belt directly below it.

FIRST CONVEYOR
A simple horizontal matte-paper belt loop carries the medium and small cards to the right.

Construct the belt from a dark paper band around two simple circular paper rollers. No motor, gears, legs, framework, or elaborate machinery.

Its left portion sits beneath the Big Stories sieve. Its right end finishes above the opening of the next container, allowing the cards to visibly tumble off the belt into it. The receiving container must sit lower; the cards should never need to travel uphill.

SECOND STAGE — “Medium Reads”
Lower and farther right is a pale-sage sieve-container with the same shallow, folded-paper construction. Label its front sidewall “Medium Reads.”

Its perforated base has noticeably smaller, more densely spaced circular holes than the Big Stories sieve.

Medium cards remain visibly inside. Only the tiny pieces pass through its bottom, falling onto a second conveyor belt below.

SECOND CONVEYOR
A second simple horizontal matte-paper belt loop carries only tiny paper pieces toward the lower right.

Use the same restrained construction as the first conveyor: one dark paper belt and two circular paper rollers.

Place this belt distinctly lower than the first. Its right end finishes above the final bucket’s opening, with a short visible stream of tiny pieces falling into that bucket.

LOWER RIGHT — “News Nuggets”
A small, slightly deeper pale-sage paper bucket collects the tiny pieces. Label its front “News Nuggets,” with a line break if needed.

This final bucket has a solid bottom, not a sieve. It contains a visible pile of small paper pieces, with no large or medium cards.

TYPOGRAPHY
The only text anywhere in the image is:
“All the News”
“Big Stories”
“Medium Reads”
“News Nuggets”

Use clear, traditional serif lettering in charcoal, printed directly on the front-facing paper surfaces. Make all four labels readable. Natural line breaks are allowed. Do not add headings, explanatory captions, belt labels, or writing on the cards.

VISUAL PRIORITIES
Make the descending left-to-right flow unmistakable through placement and falling cards, without drawn arrows.

Clearly distinguish the three card sizes, the two sieve-hole sizes, and the two conveyor levels. Keep enough of each perforated base exposed to show how the sorting works.

Favor a poetic editorial still life over a technical diagram. Keep the forms simple, the texture tactile, and the arrangement slightly whimsical but orderly.

EXCLUSIONS
No separate sieve trays above collection buckets. No third sieve. No extra conveyors. No vertical sorting tower or row of three output buckets.

No people, faces, hands, robots, screens, liquid, realistic industrial machinery, logos, watermarks, or extra text. No gradients, glow, neon, glossy materials, dramatic lighting, decorative clutter, or cropped objects.

### 3. We stopped drafting first

- **Slug / path:** `we-stopped-drafting-first` -> `.../public/images/blog/we-stopped-drafting-first/hero.webp`
- **Selected master:** `article-03-hero.png` — approved by Jake.
- **Current concept:** Research and evidence converging on a report.
- **Current alt text:** "A dense paper evidence board connects charts, maps, and documents to a central report above a desk."

The original brief below is retained for history. The **Revised Prompt** records the final direction; older constraints and descriptions do not override the selected image.
- **Concept:** Lay out the evidence before any prose gets written.
- **Metaphor (from the article):** a source set and story candidates come first; the date window is a gate; the draft comes last.
- **Original prompt (superseded):**

```
[PASTE STYLE BLOCK]

Use: blog hero illustration, 16:9 wide landscape, one image only.
Concept: Lay out the evidence before any prose gets written.
Scene: a shallow rectangular paper tray, seen from slightly above, holding two neat rows of small slate-teal and sage cards, grouped into three tidy clusters by color. Outside the tray, at the right, one blank off-white sheet lies untouched.
Subject placement: the tray in the center-left of the frame; the blank sheet just right of center; all inside the central 60 percent of the width. The burnt-copper element is the first read; all other forms are quieter supporting weight.
Details: a thin band of burnt copper paper lies across the top of the tray like a bar setting the boundary of the cards, the only copper element. The cards are blank, no marks.
Constraints: No text, letters, numbers, labels, captions, logos, trademarks or watermark anywhere in the image, and no extra text. No people, no pens, no keyboards. Keep the center protected with clean margin around it; favor simplicity over detail. 16:9 wide, no text.
```

- **Variations:** "Fewer cards, six at most, in two clusters." / "Make the blank sheet larger and more clearly empty." / "Straight-on view, no tilt."
- **Original alt text (superseded):** "A paper tray of neatly grouped cards next to a blank sheet that has not been written on yet."


#### Revised Prompt

STYLE BLOCK:
Layered cut-paper still life, photographed as a clean editorial studio image. Matte paper shapes with crisp hand-cut, very slightly deckled edges and visible real paper thickness, stacked in two to four thin layers, with only faint edge shading where paper overlaps and no cast drop shadows. Visible paper tooth, fine fiber and a gentle grain. Straight-on view or a very slight top-down tilt, no lens distortion, everything in sharp focus. Palette limited to five colors: warm-neutral off-white paper background #ECE9E2, charcoal #22272B, deep slate teal #2E5B60, pale sage #B7C4B4, and one small accent of burnt copper #C2612C used on exactly one element in the image. Soft, diffuse, even daylight from the upper left, neutral white balance, no yellow or warm cast. Mood: precise, quiet, trustworthy, editorial. Exclusions: no readable text, letters, numbers, digits, labels, captions, logos, trademarks or watermarks; no people, faces or hands; no glowing brains, robots, humanoid figures, circuit boards, matrix code, neon blue, holograms or screens; no pills, syringes, stethoscopes, gavels or other stock medical or legal imagery; no gradients, glow, 3D-render look, lens flare or decorative clutter.

USE:
Blog hero illustration, one image only, wide 16:9 landscape.

CONCEPT:
A visual metaphor for doing a large amount of research before writing: many sources, patterns, and fragments are gathered, compared, and connected until they resolve into one central editorial insight.

SCENE:
A dense but purposeful detective-style evidence board sits behind a desk surface. The board is the main hero element and should feel intensively researched rather than chaotic: many pinned paper items, clearly organized in clusters, with string connections converging toward one central discovery. On the desk below are supporting research materials: a short stack of books, several open folders, and loose sheets of paper partially spilling out, reinforcing the feeling of deep research and synthesis.

COMPOSITION:
Let the illustration occupy most of the frame. The evidence board should dominate the upper and middle portions of the image, with the desk and research materials grounding the lower portion. Keep enough negative space around the outer edges for a clean editorial feel, while allowing the workspace itself to feel full and information-rich. The central discovery should be the first clear read.

CENTRAL DISCOVERY:
At the center of the evidence board, place a clean mockup or wireframe of a report page or newspaper-homepage-style editorial layout. This is the “answer” the research is building toward. It should be simplified and clearly structured, with image blocks and text-block placeholders, but no readable text. This central report page is the only place where the burnt-copper accent appears: use burnt copper as a strong header band or hero strip on that page. No other part of the image should use burnt copper.

BOARD DETAILS:
The evidence board should contain many pinned paper artifacts: simple charts, diagrams, abstract picture panels, maps, document blocks, and other research-like visual fragments. These elements must remain stylized and simplified in the cut-paper language. They may include non-readable placeholder lines, blocks, chart bars, pie slices, flowchart shapes, or image panels, but no actual words or numbers. Use charcoal push-pins and connecting strings. The string network should visibly connect multiple clusters of evidence into the central report page, suggesting that different ideas are being synthesized into one conclusion.

DESK DETAILS:
Include a small stack of books on one side of the desk and several folders on the other, with off-white sheets protruding from them. Add a few loose papers on the desk surface, also using simple non-readable report-like layouts and chart placeholders. Everything should remain tactile, matte, and simplified, not cluttered with tiny detail.

COLOR AND HIERARCHY:
Most elements should be off-white, charcoal, deep slate teal, and pale sage. The scene should feel quiet and intelligent, with the copper accent reserved only for the central report page so that it becomes the immediate focal point. The rest of the board and desk materials should act as quieter supporting forms.

CONSTRAINTS:
No readable text anywhere. No people, hands, pens, keyboards, or screens. Keep the story clearly about research, evidence-gathering, and synthesis into a finished editorial output. Favor clarity, hierarchy, and storytelling over decorative complexity.

### 4. Two timed human reviews of a weekly digest, and what they checked

- **Slug / path:** `two-timed-human-reviews-of-a-weekly-digest-and-what-they-checked` -> `.../public/images/blog/two-timed-human-reviews-of-a-weekly-digest-and-what-they-checked/hero.webp` (long; consider shortening)
- **Selected master:** `article-04-hero.png` — approved by Jake.
- **Current concept:** A timed review by the raven editor.
- **Current alt text:** "A paper raven reads at a desk while a cropped paper hand holds a copper stopwatch beside it."

The original brief below is retained for history. The **Revised Prompt** records the final direction; older constraints and descriptions do not override the selected image.
- **Concept:** Rule-based defaults sort cards into lanes; a person overrides a few.
- **Metaphor (from the article):** 11 decisions, four outcomes (include, send back, merge, reject), a slot-cap default, a timer of about ten minutes.
- **Original prompt (superseded):**

```
[PASTE STYLE BLOCK]

Use: blog hero illustration, 16:9 wide landscape, one image only.
Concept: Rule-based defaults sort cards into lanes; a person overrides a few.
Scene: four shallow paper trays in a row, machine-cut and perfectly aligned, each receiving small blank cards; above them, off to the right, a plain round dial with one wedge cut out.
Subject placement: the four trays across the center, about 60 percent of the image width; the round dial above and slightly right of center. The burnt-copper element is the first read; all other forms are quieter supporting weight.
Details: the cards sit in neat, square rows inside the trays, except for one card in burnt copper that sits crooked across the boundary between two trays, clearly moved by a person. The dial is blank, no marks or numerals, with the cut wedge showing background.
Constraints: No text, letters, numbers, labels, captions, logos, trademarks or watermark anywhere in the image, and no extra text. No people, no hands, no clocks with numerals. Keep the center protected with clean margin around it; favor simplicity over detail. 16:9 wide, no text.
```

- **Variations:** "Two trays only, cards fewer." / "Make the crooked copper card larger and more obvious." / "Remove the dial; keep just the trays."
- **Original alt text (superseded):** "Four paper trays of neatly sorted cards, with one card set crooked across two trays and a blank dial above."

#### Revised Prompt
